modules.brief: Read, write, edit and list the files of the workspace.
modules.detail:
Reading is the cheap direction of this sandbox and writing is the expensive one, so a program that reads a dozen files to decide what to change is well shaped, while one that rewrites forty large files in a single turn will exhaust its fuel budget.

Nothing here places anything in the agent's context window. `gg.views.openFile` is the call that does.

modules.brief: Run shell commands in the workspace.
modules.detail:
One function, and the way a program reaches everything gg has no tool for: a build, a test run, `git`, `curl`, a package manager. The workspace is the working directory.

A non-zero exit is a *result* rather than a failure, because deciding whether a build or a test run passed is the single most common thing a program does with one.

modules.brief: The epic and issue board, shared by every agent in the run.
modules.detail:
An issue is the heavyweight unit of work: its scope, its non-scope and its completion criteria are exactly what a delegated child agent is briefed from, which is why creating one asks for more than adding a task does. Each issue is worked in its own copy of the workspace and merged back once it is accepted.

Three lowerings live here, all of the same shape: a program writes `undefined`, `null` or a value, and the wrapper turns that into the membrane's tagged variant.

modules.brief: The task list: a directed acyclic graph of work this agent is tracking for itself.
modules.detail:
A task is lightweight — a title, a description and its blockers — and it is the agent's own note to itself rather than something another agent can be dispatched onto. `gg.board` is the heavyweight unit that can be.

Two lowerings live here so a program writes an ordinary object instead of a tagged union. A patch's `description` is a three-way edit: omit it to leave the description alone, pass `null` to clear it, pass a string to replace it. And a status is `in_progress` on this side and `in-progress` across the membrane, because a WIT identifier cannot carry an underscore.

modules.brief: Durable notes that survive a compaction of the context window.
modules.detail:
A run picks one of three memory strategies and binds only that strategy's functions. The scratchpad keeps every memory in the window with `writeMemory` and `updateMemory`; the two file-shaped strategies keep the contents outside it with `createMemory`, `readMemory` and `editMemory`, one behind an index that is always in context and one behind `searchMemories`. `deleteMemory` is bound under all three.

Every mutation hands back the budget after it, so a program decides whether to write another memory by reading numbers rather than by parsing a sentence about them.

modules.brief: Find a function by searching for it, and take a documentation view back out of the window.
modules.detail:
This is where a session starts. The system prompt names the modules and no function inside them, so searching — by keyword, or by naming a module, which is an exact lookup of everything in it — is how a program learns what this agent actually holds. A search answers with one-line briefs; reading one of them in full means opening a documentation view of its `key`, which `gg.views.openDocsView` does.

Nothing a search returns is something this agent cannot call. gg filters every hit through the same permission the call itself is checked against, so what is findable here and what is usable are one set — while the type checker, which reads the whole catalogue, will accept a call to a function this run withheld.

Closing a documentation view is bought by a capability; searching and opening never are.

modules.brief: Show the agent a file, a value, or a function's documentation.
modules.detail:
A view is the only channel into the agent's own context window. Under responses-as-code a whole program's output would otherwise collapse into one anonymous blob, charged to one band, attributed to nothing and evictable by nothing; a view restores what tool calling gave for free — one message apiece, carrying the band it is charged to and the selector it can be closed by.

Everything opened here arrives on the **next** turn, never the one that opened it.

modules.brief: Manage the agent's own context window.
modules.detail: These are the only calls whose effect is on the conversation rather than on the workspace, and they are worth making from a program precisely because a program can decide *when*: read a set of files, extract what matters, then evict the views, all in one turn.

modules.brief: Hand scoped work to child agents, and hand this session on to another agent.
modules.detail:
Waiting can dominate a turn's wall clock, because it blocks while real agents run and the run's budget keeps ticking. A program is therefore best shaped to spawn broadly and wait once, rather than to spawn and wait in a loop.

The brief is the one place this SDK enforces an "exactly one of" that the native tool-calling schema can only check at dispatch: a child is briefed either with self-contained instructions or with a board issue, and the membrane's variant makes "neither" unrepresentable.

modules.brief: Read the skills this agent was given.
modules.detail: A skill name is a plain string rather than a union of the run's skills, because the catalogue is per run while this component is baked once. The names on offer are listed in the system prompt, and an unknown one comes back as `not-found` carrying the list of the ones that exist.

modules.brief: Fetch a program that already ran, and hand a patched copy back to be run in its place.
modules.detail:
Under responses-as-code a reply is a whole program, so a one-character mistake in a sixty-line program costs the sixty lines again. The library makes the fix proportional to the mistake: fetch what ran, patch it with ordinary string work, hand it back.

The whole module is bought by a capability rather than by a tool, so it is present or absent together.

modules.brief: End the session, in the one shape this agent's role produces.
modules.detail:
Under responses-as-code every reply is a program, so there is no prose turn that could mean "the work is done" — a model that answers "task complete" has written a reply that failed to be a program, not an ending.

An ending is a **result**, and a role's result has a shape: work reports what was done, a review returns a verdict. So there is one function per shape, and exactly one group is bound per program. A reviewer's program has no `finish` in scope at all, which is the same capability model the rest of this surface uses.

Ending is a fact about the agent rather than about the program that declared it, so nothing here holds state: the host records the declaration, keeps it while the program runs on, and revokes it if the program then fails.

modules.brief: The types every other capability module speaks in.
modules.detail: A failure is one type and one type only, so a program that handles `ToolError` handles every call this surface offers. Nothing here is a call: this module exists for the sake of the names its types are qualified by.

functions.name: writeFile
functions.brief: Write UTF-8 text to a file, creating parent directories and replacing what is there.
functions.detail:
Writing is the expensive direction of this sandbox: rewriting more than a few dozen large files in one program exhausts its fuel budget, so a large rewrite is best split across several turns.

Returns: how many bytes were written, which is the length of `contents` in UTF-8.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` for an empty path, and `io-error` when the write or a parent directory failed.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: Where to write, relative to the workspace or absolute. Parent directories are created.

parameters.name: contents
parameters.doc: The UTF-8 text to write. It replaces the file entirely.

functions.name: editFile
functions.brief: Replace the one exact occurrence of some text in a file with something else.
functions.detail:
Widening the surrounding context until the match is unique is the way to disambiguate; counting occurrences is not.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` when the text does not appear, and `conflict` — carrying the number of matches — when it appears more than once.

parameters.doc: The file to edit.

parameters.name: newString

functions.name: listDir
functions.brief: List a directory, sorted by name; the default lists the workspace root.
functions.detail:
Each entry carries a bare `name` — join it with the directory that was listed — and its `kind`. An empty directory is an empty array, not a failure.

Returns: the directory's entries, sorted by name.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` for a directory that is not there, and `invalid-argument` for an empty path — omitting it entirely is what lists the workspace root.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The directory to list, relative to the workspace or absolute. The default lists the workspace root.

functions.name: shell
functions.brief: Run a command with `sh -c` in the workspace and hand back its merged output.
functions.detail:
A non-zero exit is not a failure: `exitCode` on the result is what says whether the command succeeded, and only a process that could not be launched, or one the timeout killed, throws.

This run may **offload** shell output, and the `shell` tool's own description says which mode is in force. Under `offload`, `output` holds only the tail that fits and ends with a note naming the two files the command's full stdout and stderr were written to. Under `adaptive`, the default, a command that succeeded returns no output at all and only that note, while one that failed returns the tail. Grepping the named files beats running the command again.

Returns: the command's exit status and its merged output, whether or not it succeeded.

Throws `ToolError` with `limit-exceeded` when the timeout killed the process, and `io-error` when it could not be launched at all.

signatures.signature: shell(command: string, options?: { timeoutSecs?: number; }): ShellOutput

parameters.name: command
parameters.doc: The command line, run by `sh -c` with the workspace as its working directory.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: How to run it.

fields.name: timeoutSecs
fields.doc: How long to let it run before killing it. The default is 120, clamped to whatever is left of the run's wall-clock budget.

functions.name: createEpic
functions.brief: Create an epic to group related issues under one prefix.
functions.detail:
The prefix is 3 to 6 letters; upper-cased it becomes the epic's id and the stem its issues are numbered from, so a prefix of `auth` gives `AUTH-1`, `AUTH-2` and so on.

Returns: the id the prefix resolved to, and how much of the board budget is now used.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` when the prefix is not 3 to 6 letters, and `conflict` when another epic already holds it.

signatures.signature: createEpic(epic: { prefix: string; title: string; description: string; }): EpicCreated

parameters.name: epic
parameters.type: { prefix: string; title: string; description: string; }
parameters.doc: The epic to create.

fields.name: prefix
fields.doc: 3 to 6 letters naming it. Upper-cased, it becomes the epic's id and the stem its issues are numbered from.

fields.name: title
fields.doc: A short line naming the body of work.

fields.name: description
fields.doc: What the epic covers, for a reader who has not seen its issues.

functions.name: createIssue
functions.brief: Create a self-contained, dispatchable issue and hand back the id the board assigned it.
functions.detail:
The id is the board's rather than the caller's: it is numbered under its epic's prefix, or under `ISSUE` when it has no epic. `inScope`, `outOfScope` and `completionCriteria` are what a child agent is briefed from, so they are worth writing for a reader with no other context. `agent` names the agent the issue is dispatched to and must be one this agent may spawn; `reviewers` names the agents that must approve the work, from that same set, and is required where this run's reviewers feature is on.

Returns: the id the board assigned, and how much of the board budget is now used.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` when `agent` or a reviewer is not assignable, and `conflict` on a blocker edge that would close a cycle.

functions.name: waitForIssue
functions.brief: Register a wait on an issue, to be served after the program ends, and acknowledge it at once.
functions.detail:
Nothing blocks inside the program: the wait is recorded and the rest of the program still runs. The suspension happens between turns, freeing this agent's slot for others until the issue is terminal — done, or failed if its assigned agent could not complete it — and the session resumes on the next turn. It is how the next turn's work is sequenced behind an issue it depends on.

Returns: gg's acknowledgement that the wait is registered.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` for an unknown id, and `invalid-argument` for the issue this agent was itself assigned.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to wait on. It may not be the issue this agent was assigned.

functions.name: writeMemory
functions.brief: Record a durable memory that survives a compaction.
functions.detail:
A memory may carry **code** as well as prose. `code` is a module in the same language a program is, whose exports are bound at `lib.<name>` in every later program, so a helper got right once is never written again; `onUse` is a script gg runs the first time the memory comes into use, whose views arrive on the next turn. Neither is context: they occupy no window, are never shown back, and count against no body limit.

Returns: how much of the run's memory budget is used now that the memory is held.

Throws `ToolError` with `conflict` on a duplicate name, and `limit-exceeded` when the body would breach the run's caps — revising or deleting a memory beats accruing more.

parameters.name: memory
parameters.doc: The memory to record. Its name must not already be taken.

functions.name: updateMemory
functions.brief: Replace an existing memory's description and body, keyed on its name.
functions.detail:
Its `code` and `onUse` are replaced too, so omitting them clears them.

Returns: how much of the run's memory budget is used after the replacement.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` when no memory has that name, and `limit-exceeded` when the replacement would breach the run's caps.

parameters.name: memory
parameters.doc: The replacement, keyed on its `name`. Every other field replaces what the existing memory held, and an omitted one clears it.

functions.name: createMemory
functions.brief: Record a memory whose contents stay out of the context window until they are read.
functions.detail:
The description is required where the run keeps an index, since that is the memory's line in it. A memory created here may carry `code` and `onUse` exactly as one written to the scratchpad may.

Returns: how much of the run's memory budget is used now that the memory is held.

Throws `ToolError` with `conflict` on a duplicate slug, and `limit-exceeded` when the contents, or the index entry, would breach a limit.

parameters.name: memory
parameters.doc: The memory to record. Its body stays out of the context window until it is read, and its name must not already be taken.

functions.name: readMemory
functions.brief: Read one memory's full contents by slug, which is the only thing that brings them into context.
functions.detail:
A memory carrying code loads that code as it is read: the reply names the `lib.<key>` it is bound at, and it stays bound for the rest of the session.

Returns: the memory's contents.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` when no memory has that slug.

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug.

functions.name: editMemory
functions.brief: Revise a memory in place, replacing the one exact occurrence of some text with something else.
functions.detail:
Appending is done by quoting the last line and replacing it with itself plus what is being added.

Returns: how much of the run's memory budget is used after the revision.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` when the text does not appear, `conflict` when it appears more than once, `limit-exceeded` when the result would be too long, and `invalid-argument` when the edit would leave the memory empty — deleting it is the way to empty it.

signatures.signature: editMemory(edit: { name: string; search: string; replace: string; }): MemoryUsage

parameters.name: edit
parameters.type: { name: string; search: string; replace: string; }
parameters.doc: The revision to make.

fields.name: name
fields.doc: The slug of the memory to revise.

fields.name: search
fields.doc: The exact text to find in its contents. It must appear exactly once.

fields.name: replace
fields.doc: The text to put in its place.

functions.name: searchMemories
functions.brief: Find the memories mentioning any of some keywords, best first.
functions.detail:
Matching is plain case-insensitive substring matching over each memory's slug, description and contents, ranked by how many distinct keywords a memory mentions and then by how often. Several specific words rank better than one sentence; `readMemory` then reads the hits worth having whole.

Returns: the memories that matched, best first, each with the numbers it was ranked by; empty where nothing matched.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` when every keyword is empty.

parameters.name: keywords
parameters.doc: The words to look for. Several specific words rank better than one sentence, because a memory is ranked by how many of them it mentions.

functions.name: deleteMemory
functions.brief: Evict a memory by name, freeing the room it held in the budget.
functions.detail:
Returns: how much of the run's memory budget is left in use once it has gone.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` when no memory has that name.

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug.

functions.name: search
functions.brief: Search everything this agent can call, and every type their signatures name, best match first.
functions.detail:
Matching is case-insensitive substring matching over names, signatures, briefs and detailed descriptions, so `docs` finds `openDocsView`. A hit whose own name matched is ranked above one that merely mentions the word in a paragraph, and the query is split on whitespace, so several specific words work better than a sentence.

The filters compose with the query and with each other, and each is an exact lookup rather than another thing to rank: an empty query with `module` is that module's whole directory, which is the first hop worth making.

The page comes back as a value **and** opens as a view labelled `search results`, so the results can be read next turn without being shown deliberately. That view is replaced by the next search rather than accumulating, and `gg.views.close("search results")` takes it away.

Returns: one page of hits, best first, beside the `total` that says how much of the answer it is.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` for a blank query carrying no filter — a search that asked for nothing and a search that found nothing are different answers — for an unrecognised `kind`, which would otherwise silently widen a search believed to be narrow, and for a `limit` of zero, which is a page that could answer nothing.

signatures.signature: search(query: string, options?: { module?: string; type?: string; kind?: DocKind; offset?: number; limit?: number; }): DocSearch

parameters.name: query
parameters.doc: The words to look for, as one string. Several specific words beat a sentence; it may be empty only when a filter says what to look at instead.

parameters.name: options
parameters.type: { module?: string; type?: string; kind?: DocKind; offset?: number; limit?: number; }
parameters.doc: The filters and the page. Omit it for the first page of everything the query ranked.

fields.name: module
fields.doc: One module, named either the way a program writes it (`gg.files`) or by gg's own id (`files`). Exact and case-insensitive.

fields.name: type
fields.doc: One type's own name, narrowing to that type and the functions whose signatures mention it — what can be done with a value of this shape.

fields.name: kind
fields.doc: `"function"` or `"type"`, to see only one of them. Any other word is refused.

fields.name: offset
fields.doc: How many hits to skip, for reading past the first page. Defaults to none.

fields.name: limit
fields.doc: How many hits to return: 20 by default, 100 at most, and zero is refused. Compare it against `total` to see how much of the answer this page is.

functions.name: close
functions.brief: Close the documentation view opened under `key`.
functions.detail:
A key that is not open is not a failure, so tidying up unconditionally needs no guard. There is no cascade: closing a function's view leaves the views of the types it named exactly where they were, and closing a type's leaves the functions. Nothing remembers why a view was opened, so a type closed here is opened again by the next function that mentions it.

Opening a view only ever appends to the end of the prompt, while closing one rewrites its middle and costs the run every cached token after it — which is why opening is always available and closing is bought.

Returns: how many views were closed, which is zero when that key was not open.

Throws `ToolError` with `unavailable` for an agent this run did not give the closing of documentation views.

parameters.name: key
parameters.doc: The fully-qualified name the view was opened under, as a search hit reports it.

functions.name: closeAll
functions.brief: Close every documentation view at once.
functions.detail:
The blanket form of `close`, on the same terms and behind the same capability, with no cascade to worry about because nothing is left. It is the call for reclaiming the window between one piece of work and the next, where naming each key would be a list to keep.

Returns: how many views went, which is zero when none was open.

Throws `ToolError` with `unavailable` for an agent this run did not give the closing of documentation views.

functions.name: openFile
functions.brief: Read a file and show it to the agent, handing the program the same value `gg.files.readFile` does.
functions.detail:
The split from `gg.files.readFile` is the point: that call gets bytes for the program, this one puts the file in front of the agent, so a program that reads forty files to grep them adds nothing to the window. Two pages of one file are two views that coexist, while re-opening the same page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate.

An image file is shown as a picture, and this is the only way to look at one: `gg.files.readFile` of an image describes it without showing it.

Returns: the same value `gg.files.readFile` hands back for that window, so a program can use what it just put in front of the agent.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` for a path that is not there. The read is what fails, so nothing is opened when it does.

signatures.signature: openFile(path: string, options?: { offset?: number; limit?: number; }): FileRead

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The window of lines to show; omit it to show the whole file.

fields.name: offset
fields.doc: The 1-based line to start at.

fields.name: limit
fields.doc: How many lines to show from `offset`.

functions.name: openText
functions.brief: Show the agent a value the program computed, filed under a label.
functions.detail:
A directory listing, a command's output, a child agent's answer, an assembled table: this is the channel a value takes into the next turn's context. Opening the same label again replaces what it showed, so a program may refine one view in a loop without piling up a copy per iteration.

An empty **body** is allowed, because it is how a program says that something it was showing is now empty. An empty label is not: a view with no selector could never be closed or attributed.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` for an empty label, and `limit-exceeded`, naming the cap, when a body or a label is over gg's ceilings. Nothing is ever silently truncated.

parameters.name: label
parameters.doc: What to file the view under. It is what `close` takes, and opening the same label again replaces what it showed. It may not be empty.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: What to show. An empty body is allowed: it says that something previously shown is now empty.

functions.name: openDocsView
functions.brief: Show the agent one function's full documentation: its signature, its description and its types.
functions.detail:
Only the types it names that have not already been shown this session are appended, so re-reading costs nothing twice. The argument is the function itself, as in `gg.views.openDocsView(gg.files.readFile)`, or its name as a string.

It is a **view** rather than a return value, so the documentation arrives in the next prompt under a `Documentation` heading and is not available in the turn that asked for it. Asking in one turn and using it in the next is the shape that works. Opening the same function again replaces the view, and `gg.docs.close` takes the same name to put it away — not the `close` in this module, which does not reach documentation.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` for an unknown or unbound name — searching the documentation is what says which names exist — and `invalid-argument` for an argument that is neither a function nor a string.

parameters.name: target
parameters.doc: The function to document: the function itself, or its name as a string.

functions.name: close
functions.brief: Close every view carrying a selector.
functions.detail:
For a file that is every page of that path, for a text view the one with that label, and for the results of a search the label `search results`. Closing a selector that is not open is not a failure, so a program that tidies up unconditionally needs no guard on every call.

Documentation views are not among them: `gg.docs.close` is what takes one of those away, and it is bought by a capability this call is not. A sweep that quietly reached them would answer zero for an agent that may not close one, which reads exactly like a selector that named nothing.

Closing a file view forgets what was read, not what exists. Closing a text view discards the only copy of what it held, so anything needed later belongs in a file or a memory first.

Returns: how many views were closed, which is zero when the selector named nothing open.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` for an empty selector, which could never have been a view's name.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.doc: What the view is filed under: a file's path, a text view's label, or `search results`.

functions.name: current
functions.brief: List what is open in the context window right now.
functions.detail:
Each entry carries its `kind`, the `selector` that closes it, roughly what it costs in `tokens`, and — for a paged file view — the `region` it covers. It is the thing to read before deciding what to close when the window is filling up.

What it enumerates is the context window's contents, not any module's functions.

Nothing about it can fail: it reads gg's own live view set behind a binding no run withholds, so there is no argument to refuse and no capability to be without.

Returns: every view open right now, each with what closes it and roughly what it costs.

functions.name: evictFileView
functions.brief: Drop the contents of files already read out of the context window.
functions.detail:
Omitting the path drops every file view. The files on disk are untouched: this forgets what was read, not what exists.

Returns: what the eviction actually freed: the items dropped, the tokens they held, and the paths they covered.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` for an empty path — omitting it entirely is what drops every file view.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file whose views to drop. Omit it to drop every file view held.

functions.name: archiveThread
functions.brief: Move whole turns out of the context window.
functions.detail:
Every result carries a header with its turn number and roughly what holding it costs, so the turns worth dropping can be named: `ranges` is a list of inclusive spans, and one span of `{ from: 4, to: 19 }` archives turns 4 through 19. The agent's own messages in an archived turn are dropped; the results are kept and stay searchable with `searchArchive`.

Returns: what the archival actually freed: the items moved out and the tokens they held.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` for an empty list, for more than 32 spans at once, and for a span that ends before it starts.

parameters.name: ranges
parameters.doc: The inclusive spans of turn numbers to move out of the window.

functions.name: searchArchive
functions.brief: Search archived history for a case-insensitive substring, most recent first, up to eight hits.
functions.detail:
`archiveEmpty` on the result is worth checking before the hits: it distinguishes nothing having been archived yet from a search that ran and matched nothing, so an empty answer is not read as a failed archive.

Returns: the matches, most recent first, beside the flag that says whether anything has been archived at all.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` for an empty query.

parameters.name: query
parameters.doc: The substring to look for. Matching is case-insensitive.

functions.name: compact
functions.brief: Request a compaction: the detailed thread is dropped and restarted from a summary and some files.
functions.detail:
Skills, memories and the task list are kept as they are. gg asks for this when the window is full, and refuses every other call until it happens.

It does not stop the program. The request is registered, the call returns, and the rewrite happens once the program has ended — so everything not in the summary and not among the named files is gone. The summary is worth writing for the agent that reads it next, which is this one.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` for a blank summary.

parameters.name: summary
parameters.doc: What the restarted window opens with. Everything not in it, and not re-read from the named files, is gone.

parameters.name: files
parameters.doc: The paths to read afresh into the restarted window. The default is none.

functions.name: spawnSubagent
functions.brief: Delegate scoped work to a child agent, and hand back its handle at once.
functions.detail:
The child runs in parallel while the program continues. `agent` selects the child's model, tools and instructions, and must be one of the agents this one may spawn — the system prompt lists them. The brief is exactly one of self-contained instructions or a board issue. The child shares this workspace.

Returns: the child's handle: the id to wait on or message, and the agent and model it runs as.

Throws `ToolError` with `limit-exceeded` at the delegation depth cap, and `invalid-argument` when `agent` is not one this agent may spawn or the brief is neither a prompt nor an issue.

signatures.signature: spawnSubagent(request: { agent: string; } & ({ prompt: string; } | { issueId: string; })): SubagentHandle

parameters.name: request
parameters.type: { agent: string; } & ({ prompt: string; } | { issueId: string; })
parameters.doc: The agent to run and the brief to run it on.

fields.name: agent
fields.doc: The agent profile to run the child as, from the ones this agent may spawn. It selects the child's model, tools and instructions.

fields.name: prompt
fields.doc: Self-contained instructions for the child. This or `issueId`, never both and never neither.

fields.name: issueId
fields.doc: The board issue to brief the child from. This or `prompt`, never both and never neither.

functions.name: waitForSubagents
functions.brief: Block until the named children have finished, and collect their results in dispatch order.
functions.detail:
With no argument it waits for every child still outstanding. The run's wall-clock budget keeps running throughout, so one wait for many children costs far less than one wait per child.

Returns: one result per child, in dispatch order: how each finished, and the summary it ended with.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` for an unknown id.

parameters.name: ids
parameters.doc: The children to wait for. Omit it to wait for every one still outstanding.

functions.name: sendMessage
functions.brief: Deliver a message to a running child agent's inbox, which it reads at its next turn.
functions.detail: Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` for an unknown agent id, and `conflict` when that child has already returned.

parameters.name: agentId
parameters.doc: The child to deliver to, as `spawnSubagent` returned it.

parameters.name: message
parameters.doc: What to put in its inbox. The child reads it at its next turn.

functions.name: transitionState
functions.brief: Move the process this agent runs inside on to another of its states.
functions.detail:
A state is named the way an agent to spawn is named, and the note is the opening message the next state's agent sees. The call is bound only when a state machine is driving this session and the current state has somewhere to go.

Like a compaction it is registered rather than performed: the call validates the target, returns, and the program runs on to its end, because replacing the agent and its window mid-program would pull every remaining call out from under it. The first declaration stands and a second is refused.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` for a state this agent may not move to, and `refused` for a second declaration in one turn.

parameters.name: state
parameters.doc: The state to move on to, named the way an agent to spawn is named.

parameters.name: note
parameters.doc: The opening message the next state's agent sees.

functions.name: exec
functions.brief: Continue this session as a different agent from the next turn on.
functions.detail:
The named agent takes over with its own model, tools and instructions, keeping every capability the two of them share — the whole conversation above all, so it needs no catching up. The prompt is its opening instruction rather than a briefing.

Registered rather than performed, exactly as a state transition is and for the same reason. A session makes one succession per turn, so a second one is refused. The call is bound only when this agent may make agent transitions and has agents it may become, and never while a state machine is driving the session.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` for an agent this one may not become, and `refused` for a second succession in one turn.

parameters.name: agent
parameters.doc: The agent to become, from the ones this agent may become.

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: Its opening message. It already holds the whole conversation, so this is the instruction rather than a briefing.

functions.name: fork
functions.brief: Run a copy of this agent, in parallel, on something this one will not do itself.
functions.detail:
The copy has the same model, the same tools and a private copy of the whole conversation, so the prompt is the *difference* rather than a briefing: everything already worked out is already there.

Its handle comes back at once, but the copy starts only once this turn's results are recorded, because the conversation it inherits has to be a complete one. So it can be collected only on a later turn, and waiting on it in the program that made it never returns it.

Returns: the copy's handle, which only a later turn can collect.

Throws `ToolError` with `limit-exceeded` at the delegation depth cap.

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: What the copy is to do instead. It holds the whole conversation already, so the difference is what to write.

functions.name: readSkill
functions.brief: Read a skill by name, returning its body with the front matter stripped.
functions.detail:
Reading pins that body permanently into the agent's context, so a skill once read stays read.

A skill may be **code** rather than prose, or as well as it. Code is bound at `lib.<key>` for the rest of the session and the reply names the key and what it exports. An on-use script runs once the program has ended, and whatever it shows arrives on the next turn.

Returns: the skill's body, with its front matter stripped.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` — listing the skills that do exist — when the name is unknown.

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The skill's name, as the system prompt lists it.

functions.name: history
functions.brief: List the programs this session has already run, oldest first.
functions.detail:
Each entry carries the turn it ran on, how big it was, and whether it ran to its end. It lists shapes rather than sources, so `get` is what fetches one. The list survives a compaction, which makes it the way to find a program whose text has left the context window.

Returns: one entry per program already run, oldest first; empty for an agent that has a library and has run nothing yet.

Throws `ToolError` with `unavailable` for an agent with no program library.

functions.name: get
functions.brief: Fetch the exact source of one program that ran, as a string; the default is the most recent.
functions.detail:
This is the first half of fixing a program without rewriting it: get what ran, patch it with ordinary string work, and hand the result to `rerun`. What comes back is the program that **executed**, so a turn whose program was itself handed over by `rerun` yields the program that ran rather than the few lines that asked for it, and fetch, patch and run compose turn after turn.

Returns: the exact source of the program that ran on that turn.

Throws `ToolError` with `unavailable` for an agent with no program library, and `not-found` — naming the turns that are held — for a turn that ran no program or one old enough to have been dropped.

parameters.name: turn
parameters.doc: The turn whose program to fetch, as `history` reports it. Omit it for the most recent.

functions.name: rerun
functions.brief: Hand gg a program to run in place of this one, once this one has finished.
functions.detail:
Nothing is undone: every call the handing-over program already made stands, and the program that runs next sees the world this one left behind — so handing over before doing work that should not happen twice is the shape that works.

The first call stands and a second is refused, because a silently replaced program is a change nobody can see. A failed handing-over program cancels the hand-over along with everything else it decided, and the turn is reported as an ordinary error instead.

Throws `ToolError` with `unavailable` for an agent with no program library, `invalid-argument` for a blank source, and `refused` for a second hand-over in one turn.

parameters.name: source
parameters.doc: The program to run in place of this one. It may not be blank.

functions.name: finish
functions.brief: End the session, reporting what was done in a sentence or two.
functions.detail:
It does not stop the program: whatever follows it still runs, so it belongs last, once the calls that do the work have confirmed the work is really done. A program that then fails cancels the ending, and the session gets another turn.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` for a blank summary, and `unavailable` when this agent's role ends its session some other way.

parameters.name: summary
parameters.doc: What was done, in a sentence or two.

functions.name: approve
functions.brief: Accept the work under review: it meets every completion criterion and stays in scope.
functions.detail:
This ends the session. It does not stop the program, so it belongs last, once the change has actually been read.

Throws `ToolError` with `unavailable` when this agent's role ends its session some other way.

functions.name: requestChanges
functions.brief: Reject the work under review, listing every change that must be made before it can be accepted.
functions.detail:
Each item says what is wrong and what to change, and the list may not be empty. This ends the session and does not stop the program.

Throws `ToolError` with `invalid-argument` when the list is empty, and `unavailable` when this agent's role ends its session some other way.

parameters.name: items
parameters.doc: Every change that must be made before the work can be accepted, one per entry: what is wrong, and what to change. It may not be empty.

functions.name: wait
functions.brief: Register a wait on this issue, with its id already supplied.
functions.detail:
`gg.board.waitForIssue` for the common case where the issue just created is in hand.

Returns: gg's acknowledgement that the wait is registered.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` when the board no longer holds the issue, and `invalid-argument` where it is the issue this agent was itself assigned.

functions.name: read
functions.brief: Read this hit's memory in full, with its slug already supplied.
functions.detail:
`gg.memories.readMemory` for the common case where the search result is in hand.

Returns: the memory's contents.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` when the memory has gone since the search ran.

functions.name: close
functions.brief: Close this view, with its selector already supplied.
functions.detail:
`gg.views.close` for the common case where the listed view is in hand. A documentation view is the one it does not take away, exactly as that call does not: `gg.docs.close` is what puts one of those away.

Returns: how many views were closed, which is zero when this one has already gone.

functions.name: send
functions.brief: Deliver a message to this child's inbox, with its id already supplied.
functions.detail:
`gg.delegation.sendMessage` for the common case where the handle is in hand.

Throws `ToolError` with `conflict` when this child has already returned.

parameters.name: message
parameters.doc: What to put in its inbox. The child reads it at its next turn.

functions.name: source
functions.brief: Fetch this program's source, with its turn already supplied.
functions.detail:
`gg.programs.get` for the common case where the summary is in hand.

Returns: the exact source of the program that ran on that turn.

Throws `ToolError` with `not-found` when the library has dropped that turn since the history was read.

members.brief: Its brief, and only its brief. Everything else written about it is what a view holds.

types.name: DocSearch
types.declaration: interface DocSearch { total: number; offset: number; hits: DocHit[]; }
types.brief: One page of search results, and the total behind it.

members.name: total
members.brief: How many entries matched before paging, so a capped page is distinguishable from a whole one.

members.name: offset
members.brief: The offset this page starts at, echoed back, so paging needs nothing tracked on the side.

members.name: hits
members.brief: The page itself, best first.

types.name: ViewKind
types.declaration: type ViewKind = "file" | "text" | "docs"
types.brief: Which of the three kinds a view is.
types.detail: The taxonomy is closed at three deliberately: everything on disk is a file, everything a program computes is a string, and documentation is neither, because gg holds it. A directory listing, a command's output, a child agent's answer and an assembled table are all text views.

members.name: "file"
members.brief: A file that was opened; its selector is the path.

members.name: "text"
members.brief: A value that was shown; its selector is the label it was given.

members.name: "docs"
members.brief: A function's documentation; its selector is the function's name.

types.name: ViewRegion
types.declaration: interface ViewRegion { offset: number; limit: number; }
types.brief: The window of lines a **paged** file view covers; absent for a whole-file view.

members.name: offset
members.brief: The 1-based first line the view shows.

members.name: limit
members.brief: How many lines it shows.

types.name: OpenView
types.declaration: interface OpenView { kind: ViewKind; selector: string; tokens: number; region?: ViewRegion; close(): number; }
types.brief: One view open in the context window, as `current` reports it.

members.name: kind
members.brief: Whether it is a file, a text, or a documentation view.

members.name: selector
members.brief: What closes it.
members.detail: A file's path, a text view's label or `search results` for `close`, and for a documentation view the key `gg.docs.close` takes.

members.name: tokens
members.brief: Roughly what holding it costs, in tokens.

members.name: region
members.brief: The line window a paged file view covers; absent for a whole-file view and for a text view.

memberFunctions.name: close
memberFunctions.brief: Close this view, with its selector already supplied.

types.name: ReclaimReport
types.declaration: interface ReclaimReport { items: number; reclaimedTokens: number; paths: string[]; detail: string; }
types.brief: What a reclaim actually freed from the live context window.

members.name: items
members.brief: Context items dropped from the live window.

members.name: reclaimedTokens
members.brief: Approximately how many tokens that freed.

members.name: paths
members.brief: The workspace paths whose views were evicted. Empty for an archive.

members.name: detail
members.brief: The prose summary of what was reclaimed.

types.name: TurnRange
types.declaration: interface TurnRange { from: number; to: number; }
types.brief: An inclusive span of turn numbers, which is the unit `archiveThread` moves out of the window.
types.detail: The numbers are the ones on the header of every result, so `{ from: 4, to: 19 }` means exactly the turns numbered 4 through 19, both ends included.

members.name: from
members.brief: The first turn in the span.

members.name: to
members.brief: The last turn in the span, inclusive.

types.name: ArchiveHit
types.declaration: interface ArchiveHit { seq: number; role: "system" | "user" | "assistant" | "tool"; text: string; }
types.brief: One archived message that matched a search.

members.name: seq
members.brief: The archived message's sequence number.

members.name: role
members.brief: Who said it.

members.name: text
members.brief: The message text.

types.name: ArchiveSearch
types.declaration: interface ArchiveSearch { archiveEmpty: boolean; hits: ArchiveHit[]; }
types.brief: What a search of the archive found.

members.name: archiveEmpty
members.brief: Whether nothing has been archived yet, so there was nothing to search.
members.detail: Deliberately distinct from a search that ran and matched nothing, so that an empty result is not read as a first archive having failed.

members.name: hits
members.brief: The matches, most recent first, at most eight.

types.name: SubagentHandle
types.declaration: interface SubagentHandle { id: string; slot: string; modelId: string; send(message: string): void; }
types.brief: A child agent that was spawned and is now running in parallel.

members.name: id
members.brief: The child's id, which `waitForSubagents` and `sendMessage` take.

members.name: slot
members.brief: The agent profile it runs as.

members.name: modelId
members.brief: The model actually bound to that agent.

memberFunctions.name: send
memberFunctions.brief: Deliver a message to this child's inbox, with its id already supplied.

types.name: AgentEnding
types.declaration: type AgentEnding = "completed" | "exhausted" | "timed_out" | "model_error" | "auth_error" | "limit_exceeded"
types.brief: How a child agent's loop ended, in the six words the native path also reports.

members.name: "completed"
members.brief: It finished normally: it called `finish`, and its summary is what it returned.

members.name: "exhausted"
members.brief: It reached the per-run turn ceiling.

members.name: "timed_out"
members.brief: It passed its wall-clock deadline.

members.name: "model_error"
members.brief: A model turn failed.

members.name: "auth_error"
members.brief: The run's credential was refused.

members.name: "limit_exceeded"
members.brief: An execution ceiling stopped it: consecutive errors, error rate, or cost.

types.name: SubagentResult
types.declaration: interface SubagentResult { id: string; status: AgentEnding | undefined; summary: string; }
types.brief: One child agent's collected result.

members.name: id
members.brief: The child's id.

members.name: status
members.brief: How it finished; `undefined` when it produced no return value at all.

members.name: summary
members.brief: Its final message.

types.name: ProgramSummary
types.declaration: interface ProgramSummary { turn: number; lines: number; chars: number; ok: boolean; error?: string; source(): string; }
types.brief: One program that already ran, as `history` lists it.
types.detail: It describes the program's **shape**, never its source: a directory that inlined every program would put the whole session back into the context window, which is the one thing the library exists to avoid. `get` fetches the source actually wanted.

members.name: turn
members.brief: The turn it ran on, which is what `get` takes.

members.name: lines
members.brief: How many lines of source it was.

members.name: chars
members.brief: How many characters of source it was.

members.name: ok
members.brief: Whether it ran to its end, with no uncaught throw and no sandbox ceiling stopping it.

members.name: error
members.brief: The error it ended with, where it did not run to its end.

memberFunctions.name: source
memberFunctions.brief: Fetch this program's source, with its turn already supplied.

types.name: ToolErrorCode
types.declaration: type ToolErrorCode = "invalid-argument" | "not-found" | "conflict" | "refused" | "unavailable" | "limit-exceeded" | "io-error" | "other"
types.brief: Why a call failed, as the `code` on a thrown `ToolError`.
types.detail: A catch site branches on this rather than on the message, which is prose and free to be reworded.

members.name: "invalid-argument"
members.brief: The arguments were malformed, ill-typed, or out of range.
members.detail: A path that is absolute or climbs out of the workspace and an agent name the run does not declare both land here.

members.name: "not-found"
members.brief: The named file, skill, memory, task, epic, issue, subagent, program or documentation is absent.

members.name: "conflict"
members.brief: Well formed, and in conflict with the current state.
members.detail: An ambiguous edit, a dependency cycle, a duplicate id and a subagent that already returned are the four shapes of it.

members.name: "refused"
members.brief: gg refused the call on a rule about the agent's state rather than about its arguments.
members.detail: A compaction in flight that this call is not the one it asked for, a memory call while memories are read-only, a second ending in one turn, and a hook that blocked the call are the cases. A ceiling that was reached is `limit-exceeded` instead.

members.name: "unavailable"
members.brief: The call exists and this run's capability set does not offer it.
members.detail: A withheld function is absent from a program's scope entirely, so this is the host's backstop for a name a program reached anyway.

members.name: "limit-exceeded"
members.brief: A gg-side ceiling was reached.
members.detail: A shell timeout, a store cap, the delegation depth cap and the run's wall-clock budget all report themselves this way.

members.name: "io-error"
members.brief: The underlying input, output or process failed.

members.name: "other"
members.brief: The failure was not classified.
members.detail: Reserved for outcomes raised outside a tool implementation, which is gg's own bridge and degradation paths; nothing on this surface produces it.

types.name: ToolError
types.declaration: class ToolError extends Error { readonly tool: string; readonly code: ToolErrorCode; constructor(tool: string, code: ToolErrorCode, message: string); toJSON(): { name: string; tool: string; code: ToolErrorCode; message: string; }; }
types.brief: A gg call that failed, thrown by every function on this surface.
types.detail: `catch (error) { if (error instanceof ToolError) … }` is the shape that reads `tool` and `code`; an uncaught one ends the program and is reported back with the line it was thrown on.

members.name: tool
members.brief: The gg tool that failed, by gg's own name for it: `read_file`, `spawn_subagent`.

members.name: code
members.brief: The failure class, so a catch site branches on a value rather than on prose.
